newsitem.title: CHINA: China hunger strike dissident tortured, wife says.
newsitem.headline: China hunger strike dissident tortured, wife says.

text.p: Officials at a Chinese labour camp have tortured dissident Liu Nianchun with electric shocks and water deprivation after the veteran activist went on a hunger strike to protest his imprisonment, his wife said on Friday.

Liu had been confined to a two square metre (yard) punishment cell at the Shuanghe labour camp in northeastern China's Heilongjiang province where he is being punished for writing petitions to the government, said wife Chu Hailan.
"After he went on hunger strike, local officials used electric batons... to give him shocks across his whole body," Chu said in a telephone interview.
Liu had begun refusing food last week, after officials extended his re-education through labour sentence because he refused to admit guilt, she said.
"He is on hunger strike because the government arbitrarily added to his punishment," she said.
Officials at the labour camp were unavailable for comment.

Police in July 1996 sentenced Liu to three years in a labour camp for drafting a petition that called on the government to re-evaluate its bloody crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989.
He was also accused of accepting illegal aid from human rights organisations abroad and of trying to form a group to promote protection of workers' rights.

Re-education through labour is an administrative punishment that can be imposed without benefit of trial, and political analysts say Chinese officials increasingly favour it as a way of removing political dissidents from circulation.

Officials at the Shuanghe camp had used electric shocks, water deprivation and confinement in a punishment cell too small to sleep in as ways to pressure Liu into accepting his newly extended sentence and abandon his hunger strike, Chu said.

Family members were concerned about the physical condition of the activist, who took part in the Democracy Wall movement in Beijing in the early 1980s and was sentenced in 1981 to a three-year jail term for counter-revolutionary activities.
Liu, who has suffered from intestinal problems, an enlarged lymph node and ulcers in his mouth, had been denied proper treatment at the Shuanghe camp, Chu said.
As he was now on a hunger strike, it could be very dangerous to deprive him of drinking water, she said.
"We are now very worried about the state of his health," she said, adding that she had been denied permission to visit her husband at the remote camp for more than six months.
Liu's 81-year-old mother Wu Huifen was so agitated after hearing news of his situation on Thursday that she had begun refusing food herself, Chu said.
"She is very worried about her son... so she went on hunger strike yesterday," she said. "She plans to stay on hunger strike until the Shuanghe (labour camp) farm stops this persecution."

International human rights groups and Western governments have criticised Beijing for a wide-ranging crackdown on dissent in 1996 that saw almost the entire Chinese pro-democracy movement jailed, detained or driven into exile.

Beijing rejects criticism of its policies on dissent as interference in its internal affairs, but the New York-based watchdog group Human Rights in China said foreigners should take note of Liu's plight.
"Human Rights in China urgently appeals for international society to show support for and help Liu Nianchun," the group said in a statement.
